chapter: Hite tours, postwar L.A. and the Central Avenue scene
title: The Breakfast Club above the Club Alabam
summary: The gangster-owned after-hours club had open bar, Fats Waller, Nat Cole, and fried chicken.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: We were looking at a picture of the front of the Alabam a little earlier and you were looking at the picture and you saw a flight of stairs right at the entrance --
-- and you were saying what about the flight of stairs?
The flight of stairs went upstairs to the
Breakfast Club, which was an after-hour joint.
Did it have a different name or was it all --
Called the Breakfast Club. It was owned by the people that owned the Club Alabam.

No, no, that was the Italian gangsters, the Rizzoto Brothers (PHONETIC) and they had enough influence with the police downtown that they could run an after-hour joint upstairs and had an open bar that ran until seven, eight o'clock in the morning, an open bar with mixed drinks of any type that you wanted, just as though it was legitimized. It was run by the Rizzoto Brothers.
There was music up there (inaudible) too?

They always hired a piano player and probably a singer. The singer usually up there was a girl by the name of Betty Treadwell that used to sing up there and the piano player usually -- the regular was Sylvester Scott, who was another one of the old-timers from around town here now and he was one of the regular piano players. But, by the same token, we used to come in after we got off at three o'clock in the morning and bring guys like Fats Waller and he would sit in and all you had to do was keep two or three full water glasses full of Old Overholt (PHONETIC) which was a very well-known rye whiskey of that particular time, and he would sing and play
for a long time and have a good time. I used to go up there quite often with Fats Waller.

Then they had other good guys that would come in and play a tune or so at a time like Nat King Cole. He was a wonderful pianist, as well as being a singer. He was one of the best pianists there was in the world. He used to come up and later, on the tail end, Erroll may have gotten into it, although I'm not sure because Erroll didn't get out into the California scene -- Erroll Garner, I'm speaking of -- until after World War II.
Yeah, it was into the late 40s.
But it was always a lot of happenings up there, because they served just excellent fried chicken and hot biscuits with honey, things like that, and that's quite a thing.
